options: Explicit memorization of useful feature crosses and exceptions.
A recurrent memory over time steps.
A segmentation mask for each item.
explanations: Correct. The wide side captures direct sparse relationships.
That is a sequence-modeling idea.
That is an image task.
quizzes.answerReason: The wide part behaves like a memorization-oriented scorer.

quizzes.question: Why add a deep component on top of wide memorization?
options: To generalize to combinations and semantic similarities not captured by explicit crosses alone.
To remove all sparse features.
To make ranking impossible to interpret.
explanations: Correct. Dense representations help the model transfer beyond memorized cases.
Sparse features still matter.
Interpretability may change, but that is not the goal.
quizzes.answerReason: Generalization is the reason to pair deep learning with explicit crosses.

title: Cold-Start Recommendation: Make the First Guess Intelligently
description:
Cold start happens when the system must rank for a new user, a new item, or both before enough interaction data exists. Solving it usually means borrowing signal from elsewhere: item content, user profile features, onboarding answers, popularity priors, or contextual bandit exploration.

The key lesson is that cold start is not a bug in collaborative filtering. It is an information-availability problem. Good systems handle it by designing what evidence is available before collaborative history exists.
code:
content_score = 0.74
popularity_prior = 0.18
final = round(content_score + popularity_prior, 2)
print(final)
print('recommend' if final > 0.8 else 'wait')

quizzes.question: What is the output?
Why is cold start hard for recommenders?
options: The model lacks enough interaction history to estimate preference structure reliably.
The item catalog is always empty.
Users stop having preferences when they are new.
explanations: Correct. Cold start is an evidence shortage, not a mysterious model bug.
Catalog size is not the definition.
User preferences still exist even when the model has not observed them.
quizzes.answerReason: The challenge is limited signal, not limited desire.

quizzes.question: What is a common way to mitigate item cold start?
options: Use content features or metadata so the new item can be ranked before interactions accumulate.
Wait until every user has rated the item.
Remove all new items from the platform.
explanations: Correct. Side information gives the item a usable representation on day one.
That is too slow for real products.
That defeats the purpose of recommendation.
quizzes.answerReason: Cold-start mitigation comes from auxiliary information or exploration.

title: Matrix Factorization in Practice: Baselines, Biases, and Latent Factors
description:
Practical recommender systems often start with a baseline decomposition: global average plus user bias, item bias, and a latent interaction term. This structure matters because many preference signals are not about fine-grained taste geometry at all. Some users simply rate harshly, and some items are broadly popular.

A good implementation habit is to separate these effects before attributing everything to latent factors. If the bias terms already explain most variance, the factor model can focus on the residual structure that really reflects preference patterns.
code:
global_mean = 3.7
user_bias = 0.2
item_bias = -0.1
user_vec = [0.5, 0.1]
item_vec = [0.6, 0.4]
dot = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(user_vec, item_vec))
pred = round(global_mean + user_bias + item_bias + dot, 2)
print(round(dot, 2))
print(pred)

quizzes.question: What is the output?
Why include user and item bias terms in matrix factorization?
options: They capture systematic rating tendencies before latent factors explain finer preference structure.
They are only useful when every rating is identical.
They replace the need for any latent vectors.
explanations: Correct. Biases absorb obvious baseline effects such as popularity or user strictness.
Biases are useful precisely because ratings are not identical.
Latent vectors still matter for personalized interaction patterns.
quizzes.answerReason: Bias terms are simple but often highly informative.

quizzes.question: What does the latent dot product represent in this setting?
options: Residual interaction between a user taste profile and an item attribute profile.
Only the global popularity of an item.
The number of users in the dataset.
explanations: Correct. The dot product captures personalized alignment beyond baseline biases.
Popularity is usually partly handled by item bias.
Dataset size is unrelated to this score term.
quizzes.answerReason: Latent factors model the part of preference not explained by simple baselines.

title: Time-Series Characteristics: Trend, Dependence, Stationarity, and Noise
description:
Time-series modeling starts with one question: what structure repeats through time strongly enough to support prediction? Common answers are trend, seasonality, autocorrelation, regime changes, and changing volatility. The model you choose should match which of those structures dominate the series.

Stationarity is a central filter. A covariance-stationary series has a stable mean and variance over time and an autocovariance that depends on lag, not calendar position. Many classical models, especially autoregressive ones, assume some form of stationarity. If a series has a unit root, treating it as stationary leads to unstable inference and spurious regressions.

The practical workflow is: plot the series, inspect variance and seasonality, test for unit roots when needed, difference if necessary, then model the remaining dependence.
code:
series = [10, 12, 13, 15]
diffs = [series[i] - series[i - 1] for i in range(1, len(series))]
print(diffs)
print(sum(diffs) / len(diffs))

quizzes.question: What is the output?
Why is a unit root a serious issue in time-series modeling?
options: It means shocks can persist, making the series non-stationary and standard AR-style inference unreliable.
It guarantees the series has no trend.
It proves seasonality is absent.
explanations: Correct. Unit roots imply persistence that often requires differencing or alternative modeling.
A unit root does not imply no trend.
Seasonality is a separate structure.
quizzes.answerReason: Non-stationarity changes what kinds of models and tests are appropriate.

title: Time-Series Decomposition: Trend, Seasonality, and Residual Structure
description:
Decomposition splits a series into interpretable parts: trend, seasonality, and residual. This is not the final forecasting model by itself, but it is often the fastest way to discover what kind of model is plausible. If the seasonal component is strong and stable, a seasonal model should be considered. If the residual still shows dependence after removing trend and seasonality, the decomposition did not finish the job.

Use additive decomposition when seasonal swings are roughly constant in size. Use multiplicative or log-based thinking when seasonal swings scale with the level of the series. After decomposition, inspect what remains. Residual autocorrelation suggests ARIMA-style structure. Residual volatility clustering suggests ARCH or GARCH-style modeling.
code:
observed = [110, 130, 120]
trend = [100, 110, 120]
seasonal = [10, 20, 0]
residual = [o - t - s for o, t, s in zip(observed, trend, seasonal)]
print(residual)

quizzes.question: What is the output?
When is a multiplicative or log-scale seasonal view often more appropriate than an additive one?
options: When seasonal swings get larger as the series level grows.
When the series has exactly two observations.
When the residual mean is zero.
explanations: Correct. Level-dependent seasonality points toward multiplicative structure.
Observation count is not the reason.
Zero-mean residuals are not enough to choose the form.
quizzes.answerReason: The shape of seasonal variation relative to the level determines the decomposition style.

title: Time-Series Analysis and Forecasting Workflow
description:
Forecasting should be treated as a sequence of model checks, not a one-shot algorithm choice. First decide whether the target is mainly explained by its own history, by external regressors, or by both. Then inspect trend, seasonality, variance stability, and autocorrelation. Only after that should you choose between trend models, autoregressive models, differenced models, or seasonal extensions.

Serial correlation in regression residuals is a sign that the time ordering still contains information the model failed to encode. Durbin-Watson is a simple first pass for lag-1 autocorrelation, while Breusch-Godfrey handles more general lag structures. Heteroskedasticity in time series can also be conditional rather than static, which is why volatility clustering motivates ARCH-family models.

A useful rule is: model the mean first, then model the dependence left in the residuals, then model the variance if residual volatility still clusters.
code:
residuals = [1, -1, 1, -1]
lag_pairs = list(zip(residuals[1:], residuals[:-1]))
serial_score = sum(a * b for a, b in lag_pairs)
print(serial_score)

quizzes.question: What is the output?
What does strong residual serial correlation mean after fitting a forecasting model?
options: The model left time dependence unexplained.
The model is automatically well calibrated.
The target variable must be Gaussian.
explanations: Correct. Residual structure means the model has not captured all predictable temporal signal.
Calibration is a different concept.
Serial correlation does not imply Gaussianity.
quizzes.answerReason: Residual dependence is evidence that the mean structure is incomplete.

title: Box-Jenkins and ARIMA Foundations
description:
The Box-Jenkins workflow is disciplined model building for time series: identify, estimate, diagnose, and iterate. In the ARIMA family, the AR part captures dependence on past values, the I part captures differencing needed to remove non-stationarity, and the MA part captures dependence on past shocks.

The identifying step is not guesswork. You examine plots, stationarity evidence, and correlation structure. Differencing is not added because it sounds advanced; it is added because the level process behaves like it carries a unit root or drifting mean. Over-differencing can be as harmful as under-differencing because it throws away signal and can introduce artificial dynamics.

Use AIC and BIC to compare plausible models, but do not stop there. Residual diagnostics still decide whether the model actually absorbed the temporal structure.
code:
series = [5, 7, 10, 14]
diff1 = [series[i] - series[i - 1] for i in range(1, len(series))]
print(diff1)
print(len(diff1))

quizzes.question: What is the output?
What is the main purpose of the I term in ARIMA?
options: To difference the series so non-stationary level behavior is reduced.
To inject seasonality automatically.
To convert the forecast into classification labels.
explanations: Correct. The integrated part handles differencing.
Seasonality is handled by seasonal terms, not by the I alone.
ARIMA is a forecasting framework, not a classifier.
quizzes.answerReason: Differencing is the standard response to unit-root-like non-stationarity.

title: ARIMA and SARIMA: Seasonality, Information Criteria, and Volatility Extensions
description:
ARIMA handles non-seasonal dependence after differencing. SARIMA extends that idea by adding seasonal autoregressive, differencing, and moving-average terms at a repeating lag. The reason to add the seasonal layer is not that the data has a calendar. It is that the residual pattern still repeats at a stable seasonal period after simpler modeling.

Model choice should be comparative. Lower AIC or BIC suggests a better tradeoff between fit and complexity, but only among models that are all plausible. Residual autocorrelation must still be checked. If the conditional mean looks adequate but squared residuals cluster through time, the next issue may be conditional heteroskedasticity rather than missing AR or MA terms. That is where ARCH-style variance models enter.

In other words: use ARIMA or SARIMA for the mean dynamics, and use ARCH or GARCH when volatility itself has memory.
code:
aic_values = {"ARIMA(1,1,1)": 210.4, "SARIMA(1,1,1)(1,0,1,12)": 198.9}
best = min(aic_values, key=aic_values.get)
print(best)
print(aic_values[best])

quizzes.question: What is the output?
When is an ARCH-style model the natural next step?
options: When the mean model is reasonable but volatility still clusters in the residuals.
When the data has more than one feature.
When the intercept is negative.
explanations: Correct. ARCH models changing conditional variance, not the main mean dynamics.
Feature count is irrelevant here.
Intercept sign is not the trigger.
quizzes.answerReason: ARCH is about variance memory after mean structure has been addressed.

title: Windowed Time-Series Supervision: From Raw Sequence to Forecast Dataset
description:
Windowing turns a long sequence into many supervised examples. The key design choices are input length, forecast horizon, stride, and whether targets are single-step or multi-step. These choices define the question the model is allowed to answer. A model trained on one-step windows is not automatically a multi-step forecaster just because it can be rolled forward.

This lesson sits at the boundary between statistical model design and deep learning implementation. Before building an RNN, LSTM, or transformer forecaster, decide what information the input window should expose, what leakage is forbidden, and whether the model should predict one future point or an entire horizon.

The important bridge back to classical time-series reasoning is that window design should reflect the structures you believe matter: trend, seasonal cycle length, recent shocks, and the forecast horizon that the user actually needs.
code:
series = [10, 11, 12, 13, 14]
window = 3
pairs = []
for i in range(len(series) - window):
    x = series[i:i + window]
    y = series[i + window]
    pairs.append((x, y))
print(pairs[0])
print(len(pairs))

quizzes.question: What is the output?
What does the window length control most directly?
options: How much past context each supervised example exposes to the model.
Whether the model uses cross-entropy loss.
Whether the target becomes categorical.
explanations: Correct. The window length defines how much history each input example contains.
Loss choice is separate.
Windowing does not change the target type by itself.
quizzes.answerReason: Window design is how you encode temporal context into a supervised dataset.

title: Generative Modeling: Learn a Distribution, Not Just a Label
description:
A generative model tries to learn how data could have been produced. Instead of predicting only a class or scalar target, it models a distribution over observations, latent variables, or both. That makes it useful for sampling, density estimation, compression, anomaly detection, and synthetic data generation.

The key shift is conceptual. Discriminative models learn boundaries between answers. Generative models learn structure inside the data itself. Different families do this in different ways, but the unifying question is always: what probability law could plausibly generate samples like these?
code:
tokens = [('cat', 0.2), ('dog', 0.5), ('bird', 0.3)]
u = 0.72
running = 0.0
choice = None
for token, p in tokens:
    running += p
    if u <= running:
        choice = token
        break
print(choice)
print(round(running, 1))

quizzes.question: What is the output?
What distinguishes a generative model from a purely discriminative one?
options: It models how data is distributed or generated rather than only predicting decision boundaries.
It never uses probabilities.
It can only be applied to images.
explanations: Correct. The objective is to capture the data-generating structure itself.
Probabilities are often central.
Generative modeling spans text, audio, vision, and more.
quizzes.answerReason: Generative modeling is about learning the distribution behind the observations.

quizzes.question: Why can generative models support sampling?
options: Because they represent a probability law from which new observations can be drawn.
Because they always memorize the training set exactly.
Because they avoid latent variables completely.
explanations: Correct. A learned distribution can be used to draw synthetic examples.
Memorization is not the goal and is often a failure mode.
Many generative models rely heavily on latent variables.
quizzes.answerReason: Sampling is possible because the model defines how data could be produced.

title: Autoencoders and VAEs: Compress, Reconstruct, and Regularize Latent Space
description:
An autoencoder learns an encoder that maps data into a bottleneck representation and a decoder that reconstructs the input. This can reveal useful structure, but a plain autoencoder does not guarantee a smooth latent space that is easy to sample from.

Variational autoencoders add a probabilistic latent model and a KL regularization term so nearby latent points behave more consistently. The result is a latent space that supports both reconstruction and sampling, which makes the VAE a bridge between deterministic representation learning and probabilistic generation.
code:
mu = 0.5
log_var = 0.0
eps = -1.0
sigma = (2.718281828 ** (0.5 * log_var))
z = round(mu + sigma * eps, 1)
print(sigma)
print(z)

quizzes.question: What is the output?
Why is a VAE more generative than a plain autoencoder?
options: Its latent space is regularized toward a probability distribution that supports sampling.
It always reconstructs perfectly with zero error.
It removes the decoder entirely.
explanations: Correct. The probabilistic latent structure is what makes sampling coherent.
Perfect reconstruction is neither required nor typical.
The decoder remains essential.
quizzes.answerReason: The VAE adds distributional structure to the latent space.

quizzes.question: What does the KL term encourage in a VAE?
options: Latent codes that stay close to a chosen prior distribution.
Latent codes with infinite variance.
The elimination of reconstruction loss.
explanations: Correct. KL regularization shapes the latent space toward a usable prior.
That would make sampling unstable.
VAEs optimize both reconstruction and KL terms.
quizzes.answerReason: The KL term is what keeps the latent space organized for generation.

title: GANs, WGAN, and WGAN-GP: Adversarial Training Under Stability Pressure
description:
GANs train a generator and discriminator in opposition. The generator learns to produce samples that fool the discriminator, while the discriminator learns to separate real from fake. This adversarial setup can create sharp samples, but optimization is notoriously unstable.

WGAN changes the objective to approximate Wasserstein distance, which provides smoother learning signals, and WGAN-GP adds a gradient penalty to enforce the Lipschitz constraint more robustly than weight clipping. The main lesson is that objective design can decide whether training is informative or chaotic.
code:
critic_real = 1.2
critic_fake = -0.4
wasserstein_gap = round(critic_real - critic_fake, 1)
gp = 0.3
loss = round(-wasserstein_gap + gp, 1)
print(wasserstein_gap)
print(loss)

quizzes.question: What is the output?
Why was WGAN introduced on top of classic GAN training?
options: To provide a smoother, more informative optimization signal than the original adversarial loss often gave.
To eliminate the generator entirely.
To make every sample equally realistic by definition.
explanations: Correct. Wasserstein-style objectives often stabilize adversarial learning.
The generator is still central.
No loss guarantees perfect realism.
quizzes.answerReason: The motivation is better gradients and less pathological training behavior.

quizzes.question: What does the gradient penalty add in WGAN-GP?
options: A softer way to enforce the critic’s Lipschitz constraint during training.
A rule that the generator must output only zeros.
A replacement for the critic network.
explanations: Correct. Gradient penalty is a stabilization device for the critic objective.
That would not define a useful model.
The critic remains essential.
quizzes.answerReason: WGAN-GP stabilizes the critic without brittle weight clipping.

title: CycleGAN and Style Transfer: Translate Domains Without Paired Labels
description:
Cycle-consistent image translation learns to map between two visual domains even when paired examples are unavailable. A model can translate horses to zebras or summer scenes to winter scenes by learning forward and backward mappings plus a cycle-consistency constraint.

The important idea is constraint design. Without paired supervision, the system needs extra structure to stop the generator from ignoring content entirely. Cycle consistency pressures the translated image to preserve enough information that it can be mapped back to the source.
code:
source = [0.2, 0.4, 0.6]
reconstructed = [0.3, 0.35, 0.55]
cycle_loss = round(sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(source, reconstructed)), 2)
print(cycle_loss)
print(cycle_loss < 0.3)

quizzes.question: What is the output?
Why is cycle consistency useful in unpaired image translation?
options: It constrains the mapping so translated outputs preserve enough content to reconstruct the source.
It makes paired datasets unnecessary because labels are ignored entirely.
It guarantees the translated image has no artifacts.
explanations: Correct. The reverse mapping becomes a structural regularizer.
The method still relies on meaningful training signals, just not paired examples.
Artifacts can still appear.
quizzes.answerReason: Cycle consistency is what keeps the model from drifting too far from source content.

quizzes.question: What is the main challenge in unpaired translation compared with paired supervision?
options: The model must preserve content without ever seeing exact input-output pairs.
The model no longer needs any loss function.
The source and target domains must have identical pixel layouts.
explanations: Correct. Without pairs, structure must come from other constraints.
Loss design becomes even more important.
Domains can differ significantly.
quizzes.answerReason: The difficulty is learning what to change while preserving what should stay.

title: Markov Decision Processes: States, Actions, and Long-Term Return
description:
An MDP formalizes reinforcement learning as repeated decision making under uncertainty. At each state, the agent chooses an action, receives a reward, and moves to a new state according to transition dynamics. The objective is not immediate reward alone but expected cumulative return.

This framework matters because it forces you to separate environment dynamics, policy choice, and value estimation. Once those pieces are clear, many reinforcement-learning algorithms can be understood as different ways of estimating or improving expected return.
code:
reward = 2
gamma = 0.9
next_value = 5
q = reward + gamma * next_value
print(q)
print('Bellman backup')

quizzes.question: What is the output?
Why is discounted future value part of the MDP objective?
options: Because good actions are judged by long-term consequences, not just immediate reward.
Because rewards after one step never matter.
Because the state is always terminal.
explanations: Correct. Reinforcement learning is about return over trajectories.
Future rewards are often essential.
Most interesting tasks are not one-step terminal decisions.
quizzes.answerReason: Discounted return is what turns control into a sequential planning problem.

quizzes.question: What does the Markov property assume?
options: The current state contains all information needed for future evolution and reward, given the action.
The agent already knows the optimal policy.
Rewards are always deterministic.
explanations: Correct. The future depends on the present state-action pair, not the full past history.
Optimal policy knowledge is not assumed.
MDPs can be stochastic.
quizzes.answerReason: The state is intended to be a sufficient summary of the past.

title: Q-Learning and DQN: Bootstrapping Action Values
description:
Q-learning estimates the value of taking an action in a state and then following the best policy afterward. Its update rule bootstraps: the target depends partly on the model’s own estimate of future value. This makes learning data-efficient, but it can also become unstable when combined with function approximation.

Deep Q-Networks address that instability with design choices such as replay buffers and target networks. The lesson is not only algorithmic. It is architectural: once value learning moves into neural networks, data reuse and target stabilization become as important as the update rule itself.
code:
reward = 1.0
gamma = 0.9
max_next_q = 4.0
old_q = 2.0
alpha = 0.5
target = reward + gamma * max_next_q
new_q = old_q + alpha * (target - old_q)
print(round(target, 1))
print(round(new_q, 1))

quizzes.question: What is the output?
Why does DQN use a replay buffer?
options: To break short-term correlation in experience and reuse data more efficiently.
To remove the need for rewards.
To guarantee exact convergence in one pass.
explanations: Correct. Randomized replay improves stability and sample use.
Rewards remain essential.
Deep RL still does not get such guarantees that easily.
quizzes.answerReason: Replay changes the data distribution seen by the learner in a helpful way.

quizzes.question: Why is a target network useful in DQN?
options: It stabilizes bootstrapped targets by updating them more slowly than the online network.
It makes exploration unnecessary.
It replaces Q-values with policy gradients.
explanations: Correct. Slower target movement reduces destructive feedback loops.
Exploration is still required.
DQN remains a value-based method.
quizzes.answerReason: Bootstrapping works better when the target is not moving too fast.
